correctness.rationale: From \(\sigma(q)(p+1)=2pq\) with odd \(p,q\), the right side has 2-adic valuation one. Since \(p+1\) is even, \(\sigma(q)\) must be odd, and the classical parity criterion makes odd \(q\) a square, say \(q=m^2\). Thus \(q\le10^{18}\) reduces exhaustively to odd \(m\le10^9\). The inspected C++ implementation segments that entire interval, factors each root by every prime needed up to the segment square-root, computes \(\sigma(m^2)\) exactly in 128-bit arithmetic, and tests the exact divisibility formula for the pseudo-prime. Its leftover-factor logic is sound because after division by all primes through \(\sqrt H\), any remainder is prime. The only reported solutions are \((q,p)=(1,1)\) and \((9018009,22021)\), with \(22021=19^2\cdot61\). The stored output confirms completion of the full range but is not used as the sole correctness evidence.

Extending that certified exclusion frontier to \(10^{18}\) is a meaningful finite cutoff, especially because the square reduction changes the computational scale by a square root.

final_claim: If \(D=pq\) is a positive Descartes number in Tóth's sense, with odd pseudo-prime factor \(p\), then aside from Descartes' classical example the ordinary component satisfies \(q>10^{18}\).
